The tool in its current form on Github does orchestrate the software in Docker containers and pulls their metrics via a stream from `docker stats`.

This approach is just chosen for the prototype. As you pointed out correctly it does not measure energy directly and  a problem with this approach is:
- The resolution of 1s is pretty low
- Docker stats gives sometime out different value than top / /proc/stat depending on your OS configuration
- It does not directly translate into energy without an appropriate transfer model.

Scaphandre I know, but since it uses RAPL it has problems of its own like the limitation to Intel CPUs and also a known strong bias and very off dynamic to the real input
power signal (https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1073/12/11/2204)

So at the moment this is just our outward facing prototype and we are currently in the process of doing the needed research on our Test-Systems where we setup an electrical
measurement directly on the ATX rails of a Blauer Engel for Software compatible machine to create a software transfer model that can 
either directly translate from sensors / performance metrics to energy values or allow other folks to measure on our system directly (Similar to the Marcher System from Greensoft, only with a docker setup instead of a function base approach (https://greensoft.cs.txstate.edu/index.php/category/documentation/marcher/))

I updated the readme to make the docker step and the current problems more obivious. Thanks for taking the time to have a look at the tool.

I also wrote you an email with some further questions.

Have automatically closed the branch by manual merge of the email.

Please use not .toPrecison() but .toFixed() as the former will alter the length of the number in total

With this change the `obj` variable will not be defined on *cron* mode. 

Let's discuss the refactoring in the office on Monday

Here a bit more specification:

- A new entry in the `config.yml` should tell the tool to log to file (a filename) or be None, which tells to log to stderr
- The tool currently already logs always to stderr. The central point for this call is the `error_helpers.py`
- The method `log_error()` should be extended to log to file if the configuration parameter is set
- You can access the global configuration object as a singleton through importing the `GlobalConfig`

The resulting coupling of the `GlobalConfig` and the `error_helpers.py` is intended. We are fine with coupling the helper libraries as they are not intended to be reused, since they contain core functionality.

Can be removed in refactoring / linting.

The idea with this Todo was that the call to *cleanup* should be triggered in an automated way when the object is destroyed. However this is a semi-manual action anyway and does not save from re-using issues.

I see it now as more valueable that users just call the function than to elusively claim that object destruction will take care of everything.

summary:
This was a bit trickier to get working than originally anticipated. There were a few issues that needed to be resolved. the first were a couple bugs which were squished. 

After that though I realized that there was a design problem where it was fairly easy to get to a state where a workflow would *always* be skipped. This is because the checking steps (either recent_commits or workflow_run) would not fail the whole workflow: this was by design. What this means though is if this check finishes, and the main job is skipped, the entire workflow is still considered a success.

What this means if you have a daily scheduled workflow, each day what would happen is it would check the last run, see that it was a "success", even if it was skipped, and then skip the main job for that day as well, meaning the workflow was a success again, ad infinitum.
    - This is *too* much energy savings :-D

To resolve this, the workflow must report a failure if it is skipped. To do this I removed the "continue-on-error" flags from the Eco-Ci action steps, and explicitly fail the step if the check fails. This will unfortunately make the entire workflow look like a failure in the summary, but I believe its unavoidable at the moment. 

To help offset this, I output text to the Github Summary step to describe why the skip/failure was happening:
https://github.com/green-coding-berlin/green-metrics-tool/actions/runs/3938833624

The ideal solution of course would be a third state- skipped. This is however not possible to set explicitly from within the workflow - google/stack overflow is full of people requesting this feature be added.

The frustrating thing about this is that Github actually does *have* a completion status skipped!:
https://github.com/green-coding-berlin/green-metrics-tool/actions/runs/3938951838

Here I was testing manual triggers, and I tested a state where *every* job, including the check job, was skipped. In this case, github sets the status of the entire workflow as 'skipped'.

There may be a way to overengineer this so that you can cause the workflow to enter this "everything skipped" state purposefully on an action failure.... but considering you need at least one job to be running to perform the check I'm not sure how to do it, and it could be a rabbit hole.

Full changes:
Eco Ci Action changes:
https://github.com/green-coding-berlin/eco-ci-activity-checker/commit/10bfa1bac92cf33aee1e496ef3568d328329f097
- fix a bug where it was checking the wrong step for the recent_workflow_run output flag
    - this was causing the output variable to not be set correctly and therefore we were seeing runs happening that should have been skipped instead.
- check the [1] element workflow api response instead of the [0] element
    - this is because the [0] element turned out to be the one that was currently being run and calling this action itself!
    - This will have issues if you're checking another workflow id than the one you're currently in. 

- I had to turn continue-on-error to false and explicitly fail the steps. This is to resolve the problem described above due to 'infinite successes'
- Output logs to Step Summary so people know why their workflow is failing/being skipped

Workflow Changes:
https://github.com/green-coding-berlin/green-metrics-tool/commit/b6545017c4719501c39b5ca17406bd0c0249070d
- now uses the singular "should_run" flag instead of the two previous flags
    - both the previous flags can still be called if a user so wants to

- check_commits STEP (not job) is now conditional - skipped if it is a manual run
    - if this check is on JOB instead, then it will be skipped, which causes the main job to also be skipped as it is has a dependency on this job. 
    - using this method, if the job is run manually, the check_commits job is still "run", but with no output. Therefore the main job will still run.
- also a check in the main job to be run regardless of the check_commits output, if the workflow was triggered manually. 
- both the  above changes are needed to make sure this workflow is always run on a manual trigger

This method allows you to copy data from a file-like object to the specified table in the database, which is more efficient than using multiple individual insert statements.

csv_buffer = io.StringIO()

The main thing is that we don't want to have logins and "secret" runs on our http://metrics.green-coding.berlin as we think every run has some validity. That is why we introduced the invalid flag for runs that have some sort of fault. For example all runs on MacOS are marked as invalid as the measurements are not reliable.

What one could do is save the "deleted" runs in a cookie in the browser but that is quite hacky and doesn't really solve the problem. What I could imagine though is that we make it easier on development machines to delete runs. You can do this manually now through SQL statements in the DB but it might be nice to have a delete/ invalidate button locally. And also a filter in the front end to only show valid runs.

As a user, we would like the ability to quickly and visually compare certain metrics at the same time to easier spot any patterns/correlations/deviations. For example, we would like to compare the energy used and the cpu utilization at the same time, as two graphs in the same view.

Requirements:

- Energy, Time, and Cpu Util. Avg. must be the 3 y axis that can be compared
- these charts should be in the same view, so we can easier compare. side by side views will not give the ease of visual comparision we want
- each bar must still be able to have their legends distinguisable (so we need to still be able to have one line "split up" in different colours or something according to legend)
- 2 at a time is ok, but we must be able to switch which 2
- it must not be so visually cluttered as to be useless or overwhelming


Options/Brainstorming:
- 2 (bar?) charts in 1 view
    - Have to explore echarts documentation to look for charts that work. Could be that bar charts is not the way to go.
    - Have 2 y-axises, one on the left, one on the right. Drop down options next to each axis as to which chart it shows.
        - instead of drop down, radio buttons? 
    - Problem: how do we tell which chart belongs to which axis?
        - Potential Solutions: 
            - different color pallettes for different charts
                - Warm colours / cold colours
                - bar OUTLINE represents which chart it belongs to, fill colour is legend
                - probably still unintuitive, especially with large amounts of data
            - the charts go in different directions 
                - one starts at bottom, grows up, the other starts top, grows down
                - they start in the midlline and grow left/right (y axis is x axis in this example)
            - use different colours, and instead use something else for legend (patterns?)


- CPU utilization is always going to be 0-100%, so we have could some additional options for displays besides an additional chart. Also another problem which comes to mind: We cannot "stack" cpu utilization for runs in the same way we do energy/time. Energy and time are numbers that compound and can be stacked to see an overall energy/time value, but we cannot stack CPU averages. We will need something fundamentally different for this anyways.
    - Mix bar/line charts for energy/time and cpu
        - this only works for an overall CPU average without breaking it down per section
    - different opacities from 0-100% for each section
        - We should make sure that low opacities (1-5%) are still visible. Maybe have a "minimum" opacity of bout 10% that can stil lbe seen. Another potential solution to this would be to have a dark background and 0% opacity to still be white.
            - my gut says that this is probably not the way to go



To try:
Start with just energy/time in one axis in one of the following solutions:
1. 2 y axises, one on left, one on right. Different coloured bar charts with a different legend besides random colours
1a. patterns for legends
1b. bar outline for chart, fill colour for legend. gut says this is the way

add cpu-utilization visualization on top of this in one of the following ways:

Our dependabot was not configured correctly. It was only looking for dockerfiles located in the root directory.

This means that any new dockerfiles that we add which are not directly in the root of the docker subfolder will also need an update to the dependabot.yml file. this is relevant as we are planning on making and pushing docker containers automatically from the docker/auxiliary-containers folder :-/ Based on the issues posted above, I don't think there's a good solution to this at the moment.

But at least for now, I've updated our dependabot to find our current dockerfiles

I would like to leave this PR open and actually see if we can internally derive a concept for a monitor mode / run mode / dev mode.

We have the issue that the GMT should be also usable in a monitor mode, but also we need the functionaly to quickly burst through all the steps to just see if a usage scenario is working without having the strong overhead of setting up and starting the measurement infrastructure.
Also vice versa we need a mode to just check if the containers can get setup and queried without having any metric reporters attached and the system validated.

So in summary:
- A monitor mode that needs no usage scenario and will just "observe" the current system. Container auto discovery included
- A "usage scenario testing" mode that starts no metrics reporters, no sleeps but just checks if the "flow" commands work
- A "configuration testing" mode that executes no "flow" commands, but just checks if the metric providers and tool itself is configured correctly

When we want to now broaden this the SCI must be per phase as if we just collect the output stream from the service it can also generate values in the boot phase already and we have no means of discerning that from the runtime phase.

The point of the Tests.run_until funciton is that we want to instrument the GMT up until a certain point, then effectively pause it, and run some checks. Sometimes these checks need the containers to still be up and available for inspection, so cleanup cannot be run yet.

In order to be able to do this, I have split the instrumentation into two functions in TestFunctions - run_until and cleanup. You are not meant to use run_until without calling cleanup afterwards as well (I realize now this should be documented). 

here's an example: 

```
def get_env_vars(runner):
    try:
        Tests.run_until(runner, 'setup_services')

        ps = subprocess.run(
            ['docker', 'exec', 'test-container', '/bin/sh',
            '-c', 'env'],
            check=True,
            stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
            stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
            encoding='UTF-8'
        )
        env_var_output = ps.stdout
    finally:
        Tests.cleanup(runner)
    return env_var_output
```

Because the implementation of what checks you want to make depends on the tests, I don't see a way to automatically trigger this cleanup. 

I agree this is fragile and quite easy to break, especially if the Tests.cleanup functionality gets changed from the runner.cleanup functionality (the same is true for the run_until functionality though). I'm open to suggestions.

One potential way to do this is with a destructor:

Look into using __del__ - make the test-runner a class, with this __del__ destructor that will call the cleanup phase

Also worth thinking about having a test-runner class as a child of the runner class to inhereit the cleanup, so we do not have to mirror it.

- test_functions does the setup_runner differently now: it parses through the usage_scenario and docker compose files that are passed in, and appends a parallel_id (usually a random 12 digit number) to any container names and networks
- after creating a Runner object, it also edits its _tmp_folder and _folder to also be unique (tmp/gmt_tests-{parallel_id}/green-metrics-tool/")

- similarly the conftest.py cleanup step is a bit more thorough (getting rid of anything under tests/tmp and clearing db, and done once after all tests are finished)

- I have added a pytest marker (pytest.mark.serial) to mark any tests that need to be run in serial. I've added documentation in the tests/Readme regarding this and running the tests now.

However, only the implementation of `start-interval` would not solve the issue targeted by this pull request. Also the config `wait_time_dependencies` has to be changed (or the implementation that uses it). With the current implementation, GMT waits at maximum the configured amount of time for a dependent service until it should be healthy, independently of the defined `interval` (or `start-interval`) in the service definition. For example, if `wait_time_dependencies` is set to 20 seconds (currently the default) and `interval` is set to 30 seconds, GMT will raise an exception that the service was not healthy after 20 seconds.

For a quick improvement I think it makes sense to increase the `wait_time_dependencies` to e.g. 60 seconds. As another improvement it could be set to the value defined in `interval` or `start-interval`, if it is defined and higher than the configured value in `wait_time_dependencies`.

For reference: I have introduced this config parameter `wait_time_dependencies` in https://github.com/green-coding-solutions/green-metrics-tool/pull/568.

It would be quite nice to see a test that actually validates if the feature is working as expected.

In my opinion the follow test layout would be helpful:
- A container that becomes healthy after 3 seconds. Then a test that will setup interval to 10s and does not set start_interval at all. After 5s the test will faill since the container did not update the health status
- A container that also becomes healthy after 3 seconds. This time start_interval is set to 1s and the container will become healthy after 3s. The test will have a timeout of 5s that will however never trigger as the test will finish before. This can be reached by using the `run_until` to bring GMT just before the container boot and then executing the boot phase separately.

A container that matches this specification needs to set a healthcheck command, otherwise it will automatically be detected as healthy as soon as it has started.

Here is a sample Dockerfile that would create such a container:

```docker
# Use an official lightweight image as a base
FROM alpine:latest

# Add a startup script
COPY start.sh /start.sh

# Make the script executable
RUN chmod +x /start.sh

# Add a health check
HEALTHCHECK CMD [ "sh", "-c", "ps aux | grep '[s]leep 5'" ]

# Run the startup script
CMD ["/start.sh"]

```

`start.sh`
```bash
#!/bin/sh
echo "Starting up..."
sleep 5
echo "Finished startup."
```

This code is untested but the concept should work ... maybe with minor tweaks.

If it helps, I used this diagram below to explain how people with existing django apps can implement some of this, but as the diagram suggests, there are really **two** separate things people need to get meaningful numbers for web apps:

1. an easily reproducible set of server-side components, that are somewhat representative of a live site prepopulated with data (the stuff on the left) 
2. some knowledge of how to drive a browser with code for repeatable steps, and some understanding of the `usage_scenario.yml` file format

![PUBLIC_ DjangoconEU 2024 - Greening Digital Workshop pptx](https://github.com/green-coding-solutions/green-metrics-tool/assets/17906/96fc12dd-8d34-4062-8a3a-637d80b16d7f)

I'm suggesting something on the right hand side - so that people can start using GMT to try running measurement runs in a setup that doesn't just rely on data transfer as the proxy, but still provides a degree of reproducibility.

I'm hoping the repo linked below gives some extra context at what I'm after, but I'll also be in Berlin next week. I'm happy to chat over lunch 👍

Hey @davidmytton,

although this issue is closed I thought it might be an interesting spot to continue a discussion on the cost of networking.

I noticed your recent paper ([Network energy use not directly proportional to data volume: The power model approach for more reliable network energy consumption calculations](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jiec.13512)) which now gives a more concise approach to attribute network cost and better highlight that data transfer is not so much of an issue compared to the fixed costs.

My question: In case you would like to use the model to create a profile of a software application, how do you rate  the time when a software is not actually sending data?

Concrete example: Assuming a software is doing a 12 hour calculation job and sending the results over the wire. In your case a software would be rated identically no matter if data is sent in chunks every 10 seconds or in one super big blob at the end (assuming same bandwidth usage for both cases).

So when does a software officially count as "not using the network" and thus the carbon costs would not be attributed to the software? (Thinking here in similar mindsets as the GHG protocol / Scope 3 works).

Since plain network connectivity is uqbiquitous in your model the fixed cost of the networks would accrue constantly if I understand it correctly? 

I assume you know the time attribution model in the SCI from the Green Software Foundation? Here for instance the embodied carbon cost only are attributed to the software for the time it is actually using it. When the hardware is given back to the cloud provider for instance and "idling" it will be attributed to their books and not the cloud client anymore.

Very interested to hear your take on this.

Thanks for taking a look at the paper! 

> My question: In case you would like to use the model to create a profile of a software application, how do you rate the time when a software is not actually sending data?

If you're using an attribution model, then the software would not be allocated any network energy if it's not sending any data. If it's not allocated to the software then it has to be allocated somewhere else (the cloud provider in your example).

The assumption is that you already have the total energy and total transfer over the network i.e. you're making a historical calculation to allocate energy for reporting purposes.

If you're trying to calculate the present or future usage then that's where the power model from the paper comes in. You'd have to break down the relevant network components to understand the baseline power and what the marginal increase is whilst the software is using the network.

That's my initial thought - is that what you'd expect?

```
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, validator, ValidationError
from typing import List, Dict, Optional, Union

# Define Coalition model
class Coalition(BaseModel):
    name: str
    tasks: List[Dict]
    energy_impact_per_s: float
    cputime_ms_per_s: float
    diskio_bytesread: int
    diskio_byteswritten: int
    intr_wakeups: int
    idle_wakeups: int

    # Custom validator to ensure 'tasks' is a list
    @validator('tasks')
    def validate_tasks(cls, v):
        if not isinstance(v, list):
            raise ValueError("Expected 'tasks' to be a list")
        return v

# Define Processor model
class Processor(BaseModel):
    combined_power: Optional[float] = None
    cpu_energy: Optional[float] = None
    gpu_energy: Optional[float] = None
    ane_energy: Optional[float] = None
    package_joules: Optional[float] = None
    cpu_joules: Optional[float] = None
    igpu_watts: Optional[float] = None

    # Custom validator to check for required fields based on processor type
    @validator('combined_power', 'cpu_energy', 'gpu_energy', pre=True, always=True)
    def validate_processor_fields(cls, v, values, field):
        if 'ane_energy' in values:
            required_fields = ['combined_power', 'cpu_energy', 'gpu_energy', 'ane_energy']
        elif 'package_joules' in values:
            required_fields = ['package_joules', 'cpu_joules', 'igpu_watts']
        else:
            raise ValueError("Unknown processor type")
        
        for req_field in required_fields:
            if req_field not in values:
                raise ValueError(f"Missing required processor field: {req_field}")
        return v

# Define GPU model
class GPU(BaseModel):
    gpu_usage: float
    memory_usage: float

# Define the main Measurement model
class Measurement(BaseModel):
    is_delta: bool
    elapsed_ns: int
    timestamp: int
    coalitions: List[Coalition]
    all_tasks: Dict
    network: Optional[Dict] = None  # Network is optional
    disk: Optional[Dict] = None     # Disk is optional
    interrupts: List[Dict]
    processor: Processor
    thermal_pressure: str
    sfi: Dict
    gpu: Optional[GPU] = None  # GPU is optional

    # Custom validation for 'all_tasks'
    @validator('all_tasks')
    def validate_all_tasks(cls, v):
        if 'energy_impact_per_s' not in v:
            raise ValueError("Missing 'energy_impact_per_s' in 'all_tasks'")
        return v

    # Validate coalitions to ensure correct structure
    @validator('coalitions')
    def validate_coalitions(cls, v):
        if not isinstance(v, list):
            raise ValueError("Expected 'coalitions' to be a list")
        return v

    # Custom validation for the top-level required fields
    @validator('thermal_pressure')
    def validate_thermal_pressure(cls, v):
        if not v:
            raise ValueError("Missing 'thermal_pressure'")
        return v

# Example usage
try:
    data = {

    }
    measurement = Measurement(**data)
    print(measurement)
except ValidationError as e:

My first version was wrong. I added the entrypoint as CMD by mistake.
If we would allow `entrypoint: tail -f /dev/null` in GMT, it would violate the [Docker Compose specification](https://docs.docker.com/reference/compose-file/services/#entrypoint). 

If we want to be compliant, I think there are only the following 3 ways to have an entrypoint like `tail -f /dev/null`:

- use a script
   ```yaml
   entrypoint: entrypoint.sh # contains the full command: tail -f /dev/null
   ```
- use `entrypoint` in conjunction with `command`:
   ```yaml
   entrypoint: tail
   command: -f /dev/null
   ```
- use long form of entrypoint (not yet implemented):
   ```yaml
   entrypoint:
     - tail
     - -f
     - /dev/null
   ```

Do we want to add support of the long form for `entrypoint` and `command`?

I was thinking of then changing it to a list internally with the split. But we should keep the standard 

But maybe we should step back a step and think about how this feature would be used. We could still support the std compose entry point for people that want to use that in their compose file. 

But the main usage IMHO will be to keep the docker container running when we are using a container that normally exits after command completion. So maybe we should either:
a) have a std script in the docker container that everyone can use. Something like /tmp/run4ever.sh
b) add a new key to the compose section. Something like `run_container_4_ever: true` which then overwrites the entry point with `['tail', ...`. 
c) Creates a new docker file with the entrypoint changed. Not really in favour of doing this except if we can come up with some other things we might want to add to a new docker container for certain benchmarks or that makes something easier. But I can't think of something currently so I would not implement it like this.

I like the idea to provide a simple way to keep the container alive.
Option a and b would be both ok for me. Option b, setting an attribute to true in the service definition, would be the easiest way from a user perspective. The only concern I have with this approach is that the values provided as `entrypoint` and `command` must be ignored.
An alternative name for the attribute could be `keep_alive` or `keep_container_alive`.

So which approach do we want to take?

I came across [this statement](https://stackoverflow.com/a/41655546), that suggests to use `sleep` or a while loop with sleep instead of using `tail` for blocking. `sleep infinity` does not work on all systems (e.g. busybox), so maybe a sleep in a while loop would be the best option to implement it.

- We could output a warning if we detect that `entrypoint` is set to make it clear to the user. 
- I like "keep_container_alive" far more than my hastily written idea
- I can't remember why I moved to the `tail` syntax at some stage. I used to use sleep but that failed on some systems. But I can't remember what that was. I would propose to go with the `sleep` for now till we encounter a problem as the `tail` solution does add overhead.

For my understanding: This PR skips the sudo input in case that the file is already present?

I guess with the idea of not having to type in the password too often as this could be considered too much of a hassle?

If so I am not sure if I see this as a useful addition for three reasons:
- It increases the complexity of the install script
- It has some use on macOS but very limited use on linux as for most of the operations of the script (like updating apt) sudo is anyway necessary and as soon as we have it sudo access is cached for the file
- In order for this time saver to work you need 544 rights on the file. This is not recommended practice as it can open a security issue for an attacker to know which sudo-free calls are possible and try to exploit them. (I know ... debateable espeically since GMT is open source ... but I am thinking of automated tools here that do not google the source code)

So all in all I see more downsides than gains here. Happy for your feedback and happy to be corrected.

Hey, I hope it's fine to pick up this conversation again. I am trying to understand pros and cons of the different approaches.

To me, the main difference between the kWh/GB and power model approach, seems to be that the latter, the power model, includes usage time, because it models power instead of energy consumption. When calculating energy consumption from the power model, it makes a difference if you send 1MB over the wire in 1 second or in 1 minute. Whereas it doesn't make a difference with the kWh/GB approach. Is that correct?

**Current and future use**: @davidmytton I am not sure why the power model should enable calculating present or future usage in a better way than the kWh/GB model? The power model is essentially `P = P_idle + P(data)` for each network component. But it seems to me that the `P_idle` offsets are also historical averages, i.e. power usage per subscriber. In terms of predictive power there isn't any difference to the kWh/GB approach or did I miss anything?

**Attribution**: To me, the main difference between both models thus seems to be in the way consumption is attributed to users. Whereas the kWh/GB model attributes all energy consumption to users, the power model might not. This is intransparent to me though. It seems to depend on how the `P_idle`s are actually calculated. Let's say they are calculated for one device as 

`P_idle = E_total / t_total / N_total`, where

* `E_total` is the energy used by the device in timespan `t_total`
* `N_total` is number of subscribers served in the time `t_total`
* `t_total` is in seconds

you would attribute the consumption for the time `t_total - t_average_usage_time_of_subscribers` to the network provider assuming the number of subscribers `N` stays constant. But that is not given if you are calculating current or future consumption.

According to the attribution time model that @ArneTR mentioned, this might be fair. But it is pretty intransparent which portion of the consumption is attributed to users and which to the provider if you are using the power model with historical `P_idle`s as an attribution model.

**Being actionable**: It seems that both approaches do not model the dependency of the overall network's energy consumption on user behaviour. This is because the idle power draw dominates a network's energy consumption. But in the power model it is a constant, i.e. it does not depend on any user behaviour. In the kWh/GB model it is not included. 

Naively, one might have to think of a metric that penalizes data consumption at peak load times, based on the, I guess naive, assumption that the network is provisioned for peak loads.

The network traffic share attribution model does not model any idle behaviour, that is correct.
Depending on which "accounting framework" you image as the underlying methodology though it also should not necessarily do so.

When for instance using cloud resources the "idle cost" of the systems, if you are not currently using them, are not attributed to you.

For a network this is very debateable when and how you count as "connected". Is it having the computer turned on? Or is it having just a contact with an ISP even if no device plugged in? Or only if I am sending keep alive packets?

I think both models have different approaches and if you are targeting software developers the plain sending of data might be a better metric to communicate CO2 with. for end users maybe the used time on the network is better.

Since both values incorporate anyway highly uncertain values, and there are even more specualitve models out there like the SWD model, I think it makes most sense to only use them to benchmark against one self OR against fixed setups in similar environments / benchmarks.

Thanks @ArneTR, good call. `Path()` covers this much better than `rstrip('/')`. I pushed b67aeea174fe7784c2ba4dd10f81d9a5d80c79f1 on top of the earlier commit.

**Normalize with `Path()` in the constructor.** `ScenarioRunner.__init__` now does `self._uri = Path(uri).resolve(strict=True).as_posix()` for non-URL URIs. `_checkout_repository` just uses `self._uri`, and the `rstrip('/')` is gone. So `/path/to/repo/`, `/path/to/repo/././`, `/path/./to/repo` and `/path/to/repo//` are all stored in `runs.uri` as `/path/to/repo`.

**Moving `Path(self._uri).resolve(strict=True)` into the constructor.** Done. A missing folder still raises the same `FileNotFoundError` (`[Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/tmp/missing'`), but now when the runner is created instead of in `run()`. That changed two tests:
- `test_uri_local_dir_missing` now expects the error at construction.
- `test_check_system` used `uri="not_relevant"`, which would now raise, so it passes `GMT_DIR`.

`runner.py` already rejects a `--uri` that is not a directory before it builds the runner, so the CLI behaves the same. One side effect: because it's `resolve()`, a symlinked folder is now stored under its real path, not the symlink path. Before, only `_repo_folder` was resolved and `runs.uri` kept the symlink path. Let me know if you'd rather keep the symlink path in the DB.
